subject: owl
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module that builds an owl figure using the SDK, focusing on getting the builder, joint, chain, and part APIs set up correctly while keeping the code compact but well-structured.

Now I'm sketching the owl's actual skeleton proportions and joint placement, aiming for a stylized tawny-owl-sized figure around 0.38m tall standing upright with feet at ground level.

I'm working through the body chain from pelvis to chest to head, then defining wing joints as folded chains running from shoulder to wingtip, and setting up leg chains from hip to ankle with matching joint names for each span.

For the head, I'll add a joint parented to the body, with beak and jaw parented to it in turn. For the eyes, I'm thinking of using large flattened facial discs built from scaled sphere or rotated cylinder geometry to get that classic owl-face look.

Now I'm working out the paint colors and shapes: mottled browns for the body, pale discs around golden-yellow eyes with black pupils and dark rims, plus a dark beak and ear tufts. For the body itself I'm considering a lathed egg-shaped profile built from a set of radius/height points along the vertical axis.

Actually smoothing would pull axis points off-center and break the flat bottom, so I'll skip smoothing and just add more profile points for roundness instead. For the body coloring, I'm considering a countershade blend that darkens the back and lightens the belly based on surface normal direction.

Now I'm working out the plumage texture, nesting a mottle pattern over the countershade for body color, with a separate grain pattern for the wings. For the wings themselves, I'm figuring out how to construct them as an extruded shape in the vertical-forward plane so they hang naturally at the owl's sides.

Defining wing outline points...

For the extra "wow factor" details, I'm considering adding facial disc rims, ear tufts, a beak cone, taloned feet, and eye rings, while keeping things simple enough to stay reasonable. For the head, I'm thinking of it as a separate rounded sphere attached at the head joint, slightly flattened to give it that owl-like shape.

I'm sketching out the facial disc as a flattened sphere positioned in front of the head, with a warm tan/gold coloring and subtle grain shading to give it texture rather than flat color. For the eyes, I'm layering a yellow eyeball sphere, a dark pupil sphere offset forward, and a rim torus to frame them against the disc.

For the beak, I'm using a spike sweep from a wider base near the face to a pointed tip extending forward in dark brownish color, bound to the head bone so it moves naturally with head rotation.

I'm sketching out ear tufts as small spikes jutting up and outward from the top of the head, then positioning the body lathe mesh to overlap slightly with the head base for a seamless join. For the legs, I'm setting up hip and ankle joints with rod geometry between them, considering feathery texture via small sphere tufts at the hip to mimic an owl's fluffy leg covering.

For the feet, I'm working out talon placement so each toe capsule's rounded end naturally touches the ground at y=0, spreading three forward toes at slight x-offsets plus accounting for a back toe, making sure the ankle-to-toe geometry keeps everything grounded without floating or sinking below the floor plane.

Now I'm checking the hip-to-leg connection, making sure the legs emerge believably from the underside of the body's lathed profile where its radius is widest near the bottom, so the hip joints sit just inside the body surface and the legs visibly extend down to the ground. I'm deciding between a rigid rod versus a proper bone chain for the legs, leaning toward using a chain structure so the rigging quality is better for animation.

Writing chain and sweep setup...

I'll skip decals and SVG textures to keep things simple, instead using stripes along the y-axis for wing barring and a countershade gradient on the body to give a paler belly, owl-like. I'll skip the chest V-pattern entirely and double-check that the feet and body bottoms align properly with the ground.

For proportions, the head topping out around 0.46-0.49 with tufts makes the creature a bit tall for a tawny owl, so I'm shrinking the head sphere radius slightly and reducing tuft height. Then I'm setting up the joint hierarchy—root "body" joint, then a "head" joint as its child—and deciding to add a proper jaw mechanism: an upper beak spike attached to the head bone and a lower mandible attached to a separate "jaw" joint positioned near the beak hinge, so the mouth can actually open as the spec requires.

Now I'm placing the eye geometry—eyeball spheres, surrounding disc, pupils, and rim torus—carefully positioning their radii and z-offsets so each layer protrudes slightly more than the last without clipping through the head sphere.

I'm also setting up body colors and materials: legs in a yellowish feathered tone, talons dark, and defining how wing geometry extrudes from an outline using the paint/color options with proper thickness and bevel settings, positioning the wing planes offset from the body surface.

Now I'm fleshing out the full owl construction: setting up skeleton joints for body, head, jaw, legs, wings, and tail, then building the geometry piece by piece—lathe body, sphere head, facial disc, eyes with rims and pupils, spike-based beak and ear tufts, and extruded wing shapes with bevels tied to the wing bones. I'm defining the color paints (countershade, mottle, stripes, grain) for plumage, wings, and face, and working through placement coordinates to keep everything proportioned and anatomically plausible.

For legs and tail, I'm sweeping the rigged chains with appropriate radii, adding capsule and spike shapes for toes and claws, a small fluff sphere at the hip, and a box-section tail sweep with tapering width for a stylized flat feather look. I'm double-checking ground contact points, bone bindings, and joint/chain naming consistency before finalizing and returning the root.
